title: Sinan the architect
hook: the architect of a great many buildings, including the Suleymaniye

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suleyman the Lawgiver: kanun beside the sharia, and justice even against yourself. Your line was: the lawgiver. Which rule did you keep fairly? Day nine hundred eighty-five.

On a hill above the Golden Horn in Istanbul stands a great mosque with four minarets, and around it, a whole small town: schools, a hospital, a kitchen that fed the poor, a bathhouse, shops. Behind the mosque, in a garden, lies the tomb of the sultan who paid for it, Suleyman. And just outside the complex, at a street corner, there's another tomb, much smaller, plain and simple. It belongs to the man who designed all of it. He rests near the sultan he served, but not inside. Today: Sinan the architect.
screen: `A MOSQUE AND A SMALL TOWN AROUND IT.` → `THE SULTAN'S TOMB IN THE GARDEN.` → `A SMALL TOMB AT THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sinan did not start as an architect. By his own account, given to a friend who wrote it down, he was taken as a young man into the sultan's service and became a soldier. On campaign, he built bridges and boats for the army. Engineering under pressure, with rivers to cross and no time to waste. Only later was he made chief architect of the empire, and from then on, mosques, schools, bridges, bathhouses, fountains and kitchens came off his drawing board across the Ottoman lands. Tradition credits him with a great many buildings. The Suleymaniye, the complex on that hill, was built for Suleyman. Sinan himself, in his memoirs, sorted three of his mosques like stages in a craftsman's life: an early one in Istanbul as his apprentice work, the Suleymaniye as the work of a journeyman, and the Selimiye in Edirne as his masterpiece. What was he chasing? Space and light. Under his great domes, the room opens out so there's little in the way, and windows set high and low let the light fall evenly across the floor. Muslims gather in rows on one carpet, shoulder to shoulder, facing Mecca, and Sinan's domes give those rows a single, unbroken sky. The Qur'an's verse of light comes to mind in rooms like these. In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." A dome doesn't explain that verse. But it can make a crowd go quiet. The architect.
screen: `A SOLDIER WHO BUILT BRIDGES.` · `CHIEF ARCHITECT OF THE EMPIRE.` · `APPRENTICE, JOURNEYMAN, MASTER.` · `ONE CARPET UNDER ONE SKY OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE ARCHITECT.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at a dome. If you're near one, a mosque, a church, a station, a planetarium, go and look up. If not, search for a photo of the inside of the Suleymaniye's dome, or simply look up at whatever ceiling is above you right now. Settle, and breathe. Notice where the light comes from. Notice how the shape gathers your eyes upward. If you pray, you can let the looking become prayer. If you don't, let it simply be looking. The bell holds the time.
Sinan. The soldier-engineer who became the Ottoman chief architect, designed the Suleymaniye, and filled his domes with light. Today's word.
Your line: the architect. Today, look up inside one building you use every day, and notice where its light comes from. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Sinan's mosques, including the Suleymaniye in Istanbul and the Selimiye in Edirne, are still used for daily and Friday prayers, with worshipers in rows under their domes.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): read in full; no changes. Dome imagery recurs from 983's hook; angle differs (architect, prayer rows), acceptable.

Editor: dropped 'open to the sky' (unconfirmed detail of Sinan's tomb); varied the window-ring image used the day before; fork no longer implies Sinan chose his burial place and now comes from the teach on open prayer space; carry reworded.
Index hook says 'hundreds of buildings'; the count was cut under the claims rule ('tradition credits him with a great many buildings'). Confirm, or restore with a source.
Sinan's early life is given as 'taken as a young man into the sultan's service' (the devshirme) without naming his birth faith or dates; confirm.

The apprentice / journeyman / master ranking (Şehzade, Süleymaniye, Selimiye) comes from his memoirs as written by Sai Mustafa Çelebi; confirm the attribution and the reading of the early mosque as the Şehzade.
Description of the Suleymaniye complex (madrasas, hospital, soup kitchen, hammam, shops) and the locations of Suleyman's and Sinan's tombs should be confirmed.
